title: Gradient Boosting Quiz
description: Test your understanding of gradient boosting

questions.question: What is the key difference between Gradient Boosting and Random Forest in terms of training?
options: Gradient Boosting trains trees in parallel, Random Forest trains sequentially
Gradient Boosting trains trees sequentially, Random Forest trains in parallel
Both methods train trees in parallel
questions.explanation: Gradient Boosting trains weak learners sequentially, where each new learner corrects the errors of the previous ensemble. Random Forest trains trees independently in parallel.

questions.question: What does each new weak learner in Gradient Boosting try to predict?
options: The residuals (errors) of the current ensemble
questions.explanation: Each new weak learner is trained to predict the residuals (negative gradients) of the current ensemble, focusing on correcting the mistakes made by previous learners.

questions.question: What is the role of the learning rate in Gradient Boosting?
options: It determines the number of trees to build
It controls the contribution of each weak learner to the ensemble
It sets the maximum depth of each tree
It defines the loss function to optimize
questions.explanation: The learning rate (shrinkage parameter) controls how much each weak learner contributes to the final ensemble. Lower learning rates often lead to better generalization but require more estimators.

questions.question: Why are decision stumps (shallow trees) typically used as weak learners in Gradient Boosting?
options: They are faster to train than deep trees
They have high bias but low variance, which complements the boosting process
questions.explanation: Decision stumps have high bias but low variance. The sequential boosting process reduces bias by combining many weak learners, while the low variance of individual stumps helps prevent overfitting.

questions.question: What mathematical concept does Gradient Boosting perform in function space?
questions.explanation: Gradient Boosting performs gradient descent in function space, where instead of optimizing parameters, it optimizes the ensemble function by adding weak learners that approximate the negative gradient of the loss.

questions.question: How does subsampling (subsample < 1.0) help in Gradient Boosting?
options: It introduces randomness that can improve generalization and reduce overfitting
It increases the accuracy on training data
questions.explanation: Subsampling introduces stochasticity by training each weak learner on a random subset of the data. This randomness can improve generalization and reduce overfitting, similar to how bagging works.

questions.question: What is the initial prediction F₀(x) typically set to in binary classification?
options: The mean of the target values
The log-odds of the positive class
questions.explanation: The initial prediction is typically set to the log-odds (log(p/(1-p))) where p is the proportion of positive examples. This provides a good starting point that reflects the class distribution.

questions.question: Which of the following is a major advantage of Gradient Boosting over single decision trees?
questions.explanation: Gradient Boosting achieves higher accuracy by combining many weak learners into a strong ensemble. Each weak learner corrects the errors of the previous ensemble, leading to improved overall performance.

questions.question: What is a potential risk of using too many estimators in Gradient Boosting?
questions.explanation: Using too many estimators can lead to overfitting, where the model becomes too complex and memorizes the training data rather than learning generalizable patterns. This is why early stopping and cross-validation are important.

questions.question: How does Gradient Boosting handle feature interactions?
options: It requires manual feature engineering to create interactions
It automatically captures interactions through the tree-based weak learners
It only works with linear feature combinations
questions.explanation: Gradient Boosting automatically captures feature interactions through its tree-based weak learners. Each tree can split on different features at different nodes, naturally modeling complex interactions between features.
